---
title: "Iteratively reweighted least squares"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

Logistic regression has no ordinary least-squares solution because the inverse logit makes the likelihood nonlinear in the coefficients. **Iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS)** solves a sequence of local weighted least-squares problems. We can follow that sequence for the SuperTelicity verb-type model.

We first derive the working response and weights, then trace the numerical updates to the same maximum-likelihood estimate returned by `glm()`.

Recall from [maximum likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) that the responses are held fixed while the coefficient vector varies. For Bernoulli logistic regression, the log likelihood is

$$
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)
=
\sum_i
\left[
y_i\eta_i-\log(1+e^{\eta_i})
\right],
\qquad
\boldsymbol\eta=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta.
$$

Its score and Hessian are

$$
\nabla\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\mathbf X^\top(\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\mu),
$$

$$
\nabla^2\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)
=-\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X,
\qquad
W_{ii}=\mu_i(1-\mu_i).
$$

Newton--Raphson updates the current coefficients by inverse curvature times the score:

$$
\boldsymbol\beta^{(t+1)}
=
\boldsymbol\beta^{(t)}
+
(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W^{(t)}\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\top(\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\mu^{(t)}).
$$

The weighted-least-squares form below is this same update after collecting terms.

```{r}
#| label: irls-data
#| echo: true
st <- read.csv("data/supertelicity/supertelicity-cloze.csv")
st$verb_type <- factor(st$verb_type, levels = c("manner", "result"))
y <- st$prep_in
X <- model.matrix(~ verb_type, st)
glm_fit <- glm(prep_in ~ verb_type, family = binomial(), data = st)
```

At iteration $t$, let

$$
\boldsymbol\eta^{(t)}=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta^{(t)},\quad
\boldsymbol\mu^{(t)}=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\boldsymbol\eta^{(t)}),
$$

$$
w_i^{(t)}=\mu_i^{(t)}[1-\mu_i^{(t)}],\quad
z_i^{(t)}=\eta_i^{(t)}+\frac{y_i-\mu_i^{(t)}}{w_i^{(t)}}.
$$

The update is

$$
\boldsymbol\beta^{(t+1)}=(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf W^{(t)}\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf W^{(t)}\mathbf z^{(t)}.
$$

Indeed, $\mathbf W^{(t)}\mathbf z^{(t)}=\mathbf W^{(t)}\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta^{(t)}+\mathbf y-\boldsymbol\mu^{(t)}$. Substituting that identity into the weighted-least-squares solution recovers the Newton step. The working response $\mathbf z$ is the first-order linearization of the link-scale problem; it is not another observed linguistic response.

```{r}
#| label: run-irls
#| echo: true
beta <- rep(0, ncol(X))
path <- data.frame()
maximum_iterations <- 50L
tolerance <- 1e-10
first_iteration <- NULL
for (iteration in seq_len(maximum_iterations)) {
  eta <- drop(X %*% beta)
  mu <- plogis(eta)
  w <- pmax(mu * (1 - mu), .Machine$double.eps)
  z <- eta + (y - mu) / w
  beta_new <- solve(crossprod(X, X * w), crossprod(X, w * z))
  if (iteration == 1L) {
    first_iteration <- data.frame(
      row = seq_len(min(6L, length(y))),
      observed = y[seq_len(min(6L, length(y)))],
      eta = eta[seq_len(min(6L, length(y)))],
      probability = mu[seq_len(min(6L, length(y)))],
      weight = w[seq_len(min(6L, length(y)))],
      working_response = z[seq_len(min(6L, length(y)))]
    )
  }
  maximum_change <- max(abs(beta_new - beta))
  beta <- beta_new
  path <- rbind(path, data.frame(
    iteration = iteration, intercept = beta[[1L]], result = beta[[2L]],
    maximum_change = maximum_change,
    log_likelihood = sum(dbinom(y, 1L, plogis(drop(X %*% beta)), log = TRUE))
  ))
  if (maximum_change < tolerance) break
}
first_iteration
path
stopifnot(max(abs(beta - coef(glm_fit))) < 1e-7)
```

Starting at zero is a reproducible neutral location: every initial probability is one half. It is a computational choice, not a model assumption. `pmax()` prevents division by a floating-point zero when a fitted probability becomes numerically indistinguishable from zero or one. The tolerance stops when no coefficient moves appreciably; a fixed iteration count would not establish convergence. Persistent near-zero weights or a coefficient path that fails to stabilize can signal separation or weak support rather than a need to declare success after more iterations.

```{r}
#| label: plot-irls-path
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
long <- rbind(
  data.frame(iteration = path$iteration, coefficient = "intercept",
             estimate = path$intercept),
  data.frame(iteration = path$iteration, coefficient = "result",
             estimate = path$result)
)
ggplot(long, aes(iteration, estimate, linetype = coefficient, shape = coefficient)) +
  geom_line(color = "#1F5A85") + geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "IRLS iteration", y = "Coefficient", linetype = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

The plotted path records successive local weighted-least-squares solutions. The working response $\mathbf z$ is algorithmic, whereas the observed response remains the original vector of *in* and *for* choices; the final coefficients agree with `glm()` to the asserted tolerance. Thus IRLS is local least squares, not a claim that the Bernoulli data have become Gaussian.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Which observed quantity remains unchanged across IRLS iterations?
2. Why do observations near fitted probability one half receive more local weight than observations near zero or one?
3. What does the stopping tolerance assess?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The binary response vector $\mathbf y$ remains unchanged. Probabilities, weights, and working responses are recomputed from the current coefficients. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
2. Bernoulli curvature $\mu_i(1-\mu_i)$ is largest at one half and approaches zero near the endpoints. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
3. It assesses numerical stabilization of the coefficient update, not scientific adequacy of the fitted model. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->

</details>
